There have long been rumors that Apple is developing a foldable, clamshell-style device — possibly an iPad, a Mac, or both, or some hybrid of the two.

Recently there have been reports claiming this project has been cancelled, even though it has long been a priority for incoming CEO John Ternus — but I don't think that's entirely accurate…

Personally, I think the concept of a Mac/iPad hybrid is basically outdated. Macs can now run iPhone and iPad apps, and for many people iPhone Mirroring already does something similar. We're also seeing increasing convergence between the two operating systems, and I believe that trend will continue: Apple's old "toaster-fridge" debate is well and truly over.

But I do believe that, one day, we will have an all-screen foldable Mac — provided the technology matures enough for a soft keyboard to genuinely replace a hard one. That won't happen any time soon, but it will eventually happen.

The transition phase of the dynamic keyboard

I think we're still a long way from that day, because I believe we'll go through an intermediate phase first: the dynamic hardware keyboard. I argued around a decade ago why I thought this was the future; although it's now in use in some niche applications, it hasn't yet entered the mainstream.

An early example is the Sonder Keyboard, which uses small e-ink displays to relabel and remap keys.

For example, for someone who spends their day cutting video in Final Cut Pro, a QWERTY keyboard is essentially useless — which is why physical keyboards and keyboard covers exist.

Wouldn't it be smarter if our MacBook keyboards, or our desktop Magic Keyboards, could automatically relabel themselves according to the application being used at that moment?

A soft keyboard that feels like a hard one

However, the long-term goal is a fully soft keyboard. Back in 2016, I made the point that the argument Steve Jobs made for virtual keys when launching the iPhone applies equally to the Mac keyboard.

Of course, there are three problems with soft keyboards:

  • Glass keyboards are uncomfortable to type on
  • We rely on key travel for feedback and comfort
  • Touch typists need to feel the location of keys before pressing them

Apple has already obtained patents addressing each of these three problems. First, using a flexible display rather than conventional glass allows the surface to deform when a virtual key is pressed. The second problem can be addressed by combining this deformation with haptic motors. And the third — the need to physically feel the keys — can be tackled in two ways.

Apple's patent uses electrostatic charge to make the user perceive changes in surface texture. In other words, the surface can remain flat, but by applying a charge to the display surface, it can create the sensation of a physical key. In 2023, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University proposed another approach.

It's a question of when, not if

Of course, all of this is still at a very early stage, but we only need to look at the Mac trackpad. Trackpads still sound and feel like mechanical devices, but in reality they have for years been solid-state components using haptic feedback to simulate a physical click — and remarkably convincingly at that.

Soft keyboards will one day reach the same level of maturity. Whether through Apple's current approach or through technologies not yet seen, they will solve these three problems.

On that day, Steve's argument will apply to the Mac in exactly the same way. In clamshell mode, the keyboard will appear in whatever form is best suited to the current task. When we simply want a giant screen — whether for watching movies or drawing with the Apple Pencil — we just open it up and get double the screen area.

So I'm perfectly happy to accept the claim that the first-generation device may have been shelved for now, but that absolutely does not equate to saying it's been cancelled. The time for this technology will come.

That's my view — what's yours? Please share your thoughts in the comments section.
